parts: Classic pumpkin pie from scratch: the Thanksgiving recipe, step by step.
A silky, deep-orange custard in a flaky butter crust, baked the day before so the oven is free on the big day.
Plus the small Illinois town behind almost every can of pumpkin, and the 1796 cookbook that started it all.
Pumpkin pie is the dessert most of us eat one day a year and argue about the rest.
Too spicy, too sweet, cracked down the middle, soggy on the bottom.
The truth is kinder: a great one comes down to cold butter, two oven temperatures and the patience to let it cool.
This is the classic: a smooth, gently spiced custard in a flaky crust that stays crisp.
Make it the day before Thanksgiving, Thursday, November 26, 2026.
It tastes even better after a night in the fridge.
The recipe at a glance.
Serves: 8. Prep: 30 minutes, plus 1 hour to chill the dough.
Bake: 55 to 65 minutes. Oven: 425 degrees Fahrenheit, then 350 degrees Fahrenheit.
Ingredients: butter crust.
1¼ cups, All-purpose flour, plus ½ teaspoon salt
½ cup (1 stick), Cold unsalted butter, cut into small cubes
3 to 4 tablespoons, Ice water
Ingredients: pumpkin filling.
1 can (15 ounces), 100% pure pumpkin (not pumpkin pie filling)
1 can (12 ounces), Evaporated milk
2 large, plus 1 yolk, Eggs
¾ cup, packed, Dark brown sugar
2 teaspoons, Pumpkin pie spice
½ teaspoon, Kosher salt
1 teaspoon, Pure vanilla extract
Tools.
9-inch pie dish: A deep, even custard
French rolling pin: Rolling the dough thin and round
Pastry blender: Cutting cold butter into the flour
Hand mixer or a whisk: A smooth filling with no lumps
Pie server: Clean slices at the table
Steps: the crust.
Step 1. Mix the flour and salt. Cut in the cold butter until the pieces are the size of peas.
Step 2. Sprinkle in ice water, 1 tablespoon at a time, tossing with a fork until the dough just holds together.
Step 3. Press into a flat disk, wrap it and chill for 1 hour.
Step 4. Roll into a 12-inch circle. Ease it into the dish, fold the edge under and crimp.
Step 5. Chill the crust 15 minutes while the oven heats to 425 degrees Fahrenheit.
Steps: the filling and bake.
Step 1. Whisk the eggs and yolk in a large bowl.
Step 2. Add the pumpkin, brown sugar, spice, salt and vanilla.
Mix until smooth.
Step 3. Slowly mix in the evaporated milk.
Step 4. Set the crust on a baking sheet and pour in the filling.
Step 5. Bake 15 minutes at 425 degrees Fahrenheit.
Step 6. Lower the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit. Bake 40 to 50 minutes more, until the edge is set, the center still wobbles a little and a knife slid in an inch from the center comes out clean.
Step 7. Crust browning too fast? Cover the edge with a ring of foil.
Step 8. Cool on a rack for at least 2 hours.
The center firms up as it cools.
Why two temperatures.
The hot start is for the crust. Fifteen minutes at 425 degrees Fahrenheit sets the bottom and the edge before the wet filling can soak in, which is the whole secret to a crust that isn’t soggy.
Then the heat drops, because the filling is a custard: eggs and milk that thicken gently.
Rush it and the eggs tighten too far, and the top cracks like dry earth.
Cold butter is the other half of the story.
Little pieces of butter melt in the oven and leave pockets of steam, and those pockets are the flakes.
A pastry blender cuts the butter in without warming it the way your hands would.
If the dough gets soft while you roll, put it back in the fridge for ten minutes.
It always forgives you.
The town that cans America’s pumpkin.
Look closely at the pumpkin in the can. It isn’t the round orange jack-o’-lantern kind.
Most of it is a tan-skinned variety called the Dickinson, which looks and tastes more like a butternut squash.
That’s a good thing: its flesh is dense, sweet and smooth, perfect for pie.
And most of it comes from one place.

About 90% of the canned pumpkin made in the United States is grown within 60 miles of Morton, Illinois, the self-proclaimed Pumpkin Capital of the World, where the Libby’s plant runs around the clock in season.
Libby’s, which began in Chicago canning corned beef after the Civil War, bought Dickinson’s pumpkin business in 1929, moved to Morton in 1960, and has belonged to Nestlé since 1976.
In 2025 Illinois grew 535 million pounds of pumpkins, the U.
S. Department of Agriculture says, more than the next four states combined.
The 1796 “pompkin”.
The first custard-style pumpkin pie on record comes from American Cookery by Amelia Simmons, published in 1796 and believed to be the first cookbook written by an American.
Her “pompkin” pudding mixed stewed pumpkin with cream, eggs, sugar, nutmeg, mace and ginger, baked in a crust for 45 minutes.
She gave no exact amounts for the spices, so every cook since has been adjusting to taste.
English cooks were already baking pumpkin into pies, but in slices under a top crust.
The smooth, open custard is an American idea, and it has sat on Thanksgiving tables ever since the day became a national holiday in 1863.
Make it ahead, serve it right.
Bake the pie a day early. Once it has cooled completely, cover it and keep it in the fridge, because the filling is made with eggs and milk.
Take it out an hour before dessert, and stir a teaspoon of pure vanilla into the whipped cream.
Cut with a thin, sharp pie server, wiping it clean between slices, and every piece comes out like the picture.
Maple whipped cream: Whip 1 cup cold heavy cream with 2 tablespoons pure maple syrup
Toasted pecans: Toast pecan halves 5 minutes in a dry pan and scatter on top
